title: Floorplan Intelligence
notes: A conversation between James (British, lead) and Ava (American). Text in [brackets] is an ElevenLabs v3 audio tag; voice.py strips tags for models that don't support them. 'short: false' segments are dropped from the short cut (assemble.py --short). 'caption' is an on-screen lower third. 'visual.file' paths are relative to presentation/demo/.

lines.text: Ava, every building starts the same way, doesn't it?
With a sentence. A clinic with six exam rooms. A twenty-megawatt AI factory.
And then weeks of drawings, before anyone knows if it actually works.
So we asked ourselves... [softly] what if the sentence was enough?
This is Floorplan Intelligence.
Brief in. Building out.
Now, James, the obvious move is to just ask an AI to draw the plan, right?
We tried that. It draws one, very confidently. Rooms overlap. The corridor comes out ten times too wide. And then it tells you it's code-compliant.
And a constraint solver?
The opposite. Flawless geometry. But it can't read a single word of your brief.
So we split the job, by what each tool is genuinely good at.
NVIDIA Nemotron reads the intent. A solver makes the geometry exact. A rule checker cites what passed.
And the browser lets anyone walk it, stress it, and price it.
The model proposes.
The solver proves.
And the simulator tells you if it works.
Let's start with the model. James, why Nemotron?

Nemotron Nano. Nine billion parameters, and it's a hybrid: mostly Mamba-2 state-space layers, which read long context in linear time, with attention only where it matters. Small enough to run on a laptop.
And you didn't just use it off the shelf.
No. Two stages. First, Q-LoRA fine-tuning, on four hundred solver-certified clinic layouts, written in a compact plan language we designed for it.
Then reinforcement learning, with GRPO.
Right, and with no human preference model. Four rewards, computed straight from the plan. Does it parse? Do rooms overlap? Can you reach every room? Does it meet the code?
So the plan itself grades the model.
And when it generates, there's a grammar running inside llama-C-P-P.
Which means every token it writes has to be legal. Every single line parses.
But then you tested it properly.

We did, and here's the honest part. The room program was right, every time: which rooms, and how many. The coordinates were not. A corridor of eighteen hundred millimetres came out at eighteen thousand.
So the model writes the program, and the geometry goes to a solver.
Ava, walk us through the solver.

Google OR-Tools CP-SAT, on a hundred-millimetre grid. Every room becomes integer variables. No two rooms can overlap, by construction. Locked rooms stay exactly where you put them, and rooms joined by a door must share a wall.
And everything else?
Moves as little as possible. That's the objective.
And when you ask for something impossible?
It doesn't make something up. It returns a proof: the smallest set of rooms that can't all fit, and the arithmetic why.
Then nine rules are checked. ADA door widths and turning circles, FGI exam-room sizes, IBC egress. Each one with the measured value, the requirement, and the citation.
We never say compliant. We say exactly what passed.
And the 3D comes from just rooms and doors?
Just rooms and doors. The viewer derives the walls, the windows, the furniture, a walkable grid, and real A-star walking paths.
Which keeps the simulation honest. Move the nurse station, and the nurses really do walk further.
Then we simulate the day. It's a discrete-event engine. Patients, nurses, providers and the front desk, and every visit is a chain of events on a timeline.
Check in, wait, vitals, the provider, checkout. And it's seeded, so it's deterministic: same seed, same day, down to the minute.
And we don't run one day. We run twenty, so you get a range, not a guess.
And none of this is a mock-up.

Two apps on one pipeline. About twenty-two thousand lines of TypeScript, five and a half thousand of Python, and two hundred and ten tests, including golden files that freeze the simulator's numbers to the minute.
Running in the browser, on WebGPU.
Okay. Enough diagrams.
[laughs] Let's see it.
I'm describing a primary-care clinic. Six exam rooms, a nurse station, an accessible restroom. Generate.
Three candidates, ranked by the checks they pass. Nine out of nine, all three.

segments.caption: Recorded with the model off: a deterministic parser writes the room program. With Nemotron on, about 47 s on an M4 Pro.

lines.text: Open one, and it's a building.
Rendered live, in the browser. Click a room and it tells you what it's for. Or take the guided tour, in the order a patient walks it.
Now, the real question. Does it cope with flu season?
Flu-season Monday. Ninety patients, and a morning rush. Run twenty days.
And there's the verdict, in plain words, with the bottleneck.
What if we add a nurse?
The assistant changes the day, runs it again, and comes back with the new wait.
And it never guesses. Every number comes from the same engine you see on screen.
Can we compare the layouts?
Same day, every plan, side by side.
And edits are just plain language. Make the waiting room twenty percent bigger, and keep the restrooms where they are.
The solver keeps what you asked for, and moves the rest.
And if I ask for something impossible?
It tells you exactly why.
Then export everything. A 3D model, the plan, the drawing, and a script that builds it in Blender.
Now, this is my favourite part. Same model. Same solver. Same viewer...
[excited] ...and a completely different building.
A twenty-megawatt AI factory. Liquid cooled. N plus one cooling, two-N power.
Three designs: liquid, hybrid, and air. Every rack, cooler, UPS and generator, placed.
And CP-SAT proves the layout, in about thirty milliseconds.
Then four lenses, each answering one question. Where does the power go? Where does it get hot? And what keeps running if something breaks?
So how does it know what keeps running?
Plain capacity arithmetic, over every power and cooling path. Lose a cooler, and the three that are left carry twenty-four hundred kilowatts, against a load of twenty-one hundred.
So it's still up, but with no backup left.
Exactly. And a thermal estimate shows where the heat builds up.
So, let's break it. The grid goes down.
And the generators take over.
Worst day, then. Grid down, a generator fails, and it's forty-two degrees outside.
And you can see exactly which racks go dark, and why.
And what does all of this cost?
To build, and to run. Where every kilowatt-hour goes. Dollars per GPU-hour.
Change the electricity price, and everything updates.
And it exports to OpenUSD, straight into NVIDIA Omniverse, with every part's power and path attached.
So, James. Does it actually hold up?
Twenty out of twenty test briefs accepted, with every check passing. Five out of five impossible requests answered with a proof, not a plan.
And it all runs on a laptop. A five-and-a-half-gigabyte model, and no data leaves the machine.
And no cost per plan.
So who's it for?
Health systems, testing a clinic before they sign the lease.
Architects, with a checked first plan in minutes, instead of days.
And AI infrastructure teams, comparing liquid against air, and seeing what survives a heat wave.
And the next building type is a config pack, not a new product. Schools. Offices. Warehouses. Labs.
From a sentence...
...to a building you can walk, stress, and price.
This is Floorplan Intelligence.
Built for the Nebius and NVIDIA Global AI Hackathon. [warmly] Thank you.
